title: Case Report or Research? Exemption Calls and Anonymous vs De-identified Data
summary: Learn where a case report ends and research begins under the US Common Rule, why the case-count threshold and the exemption decision are set by local policy, and how anonymous, anonymized, coded and HIPAA de-identified data differ.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 14 Hit 6 and Traps 2, 3 and 5. Regulatory points from the Common Rule (45 CFR 46.102, 46.103, 46.104) and HIPAA (45 CFR 164.514), eCFR version 2026-10-01; case-report practice from Bass 2020 and Valešić 2025; data-coding terms from ICH E15 as issued by FDA (2008). The reviewer’s “a second case = research” is a local-policy threshold, not a federal rule (register flag rv-case-report-local-threshold). The reviewer’s “exempt studies use deidentified data” omits exempt categories for identifiable data (rv-exempt-identifiable-categories). HIPAA de-identified data may keep a re-identification code (rv-deidentified-code-key). Who decides exemption follows the existing flag rv-exempt-determiner. OHRP guidance pages were not read (blocked for an earlier lesson; not retried). Not taught: trial phases, Moore v. UCLA, kickbacks, research billing, retention periods.

objectives: Explain why a single descriptive case report is generally not human subjects research and why the threshold for a case series is set locally.
State that the Common Rule lists exempt categories without naming who decides, so institutional policy governs the exemption call.
Distinguish identified, coded, anonymized, anonymous and HIPAA de-identified data.

scenes.title: One case, then two, then a spreadsheet
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a laboratory scientist finds a striking, rare result pattern in one patient and wants to write it up. Weeks later a second patient shows the same pattern. A colleague then proposes pulling five years of records into a spreadsheet with names removed, and says: “I have decided it is exempt, so we can start today.” Question token: “Which step needs the IRB?”

cues.text: Invented scenario: a lab scientist sees a rare result pattern in one patient and wants to write it up as a case report.
A second patient shows the same pattern. Then a colleague wants to pull five years of records, names removed, and says: I have decided it is exempt, let us start today.
Which of these steps needs the IRB, and who gets to decide?

props.label: Which step needs the IRB? Who decides?

scenes.title: Where research begins
scenes.altText: Two definition cards from the US Common Rule (45 CFR 46.102). Research: a systematic investigation designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge. Human subject: a living individual about whom an investigator obtains information through intervention or interaction, or obtains, uses or analyzes identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens. Case-report card: a case report limited to describing one patient’s clinical features, with no contribution to generalizable knowledge, is generally not human subjects research, and many institutions and jurisdictions do not treat a single case report as research. Consent card: whether ethics approval is needed and whether the patient consented to publication of personal details are two separate questions, and many journals require a consent statement.

cues.text: Under the US Common Rule, research is a systematic investigation designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge.
A human subject includes a living person whose identifiable private information an investigator obtains or analyzes. A medical record counts as private information.
A single case report that only describes one patient’s clinical features is generally not human subjects research, and many institutions do not treat it as research.
But two questions stay separate: does it need ethics review, and did the patient consent to having their details published? Many journals require a consent statement.

scenes.title: From anecdote to investigation
scenes.altText: Threshold card: the US regulations do not define how many cases turn a report into research; most IRBs set locally both how many cases are not research and the threshold at which a series becomes systematic investigation. Policy card: practice varies — some institutions require a formal IRB exemption letter even for a single case report, others leave it to authors or department heads. Timing token: federally supported research covered by the Common Rule may not be initiated before IRB approval is certified (46.103(d)). Exemption card: 45 CFR 46.104 lists exempt categories but its text does not name who makes the determination; that is set by institutional policy, and some institutions require a formal IRB exemption letter.

cues.text: How many cases make research? The federal regulations do not say. Most IRBs set a local threshold at which a case series becomes systematic investigation.
Institutions differ: some want a formal IRB exemption letter even for one case, while others leave the call to authors or department heads.
Timing matters. Federally supported research covered by the Common Rule may not begin until IRB approval is certified, so check before pulling records.
And exemption? The regulation lists exempt categories, but it does not name who decides. Your institution’s policy does, and some institutions require a formal IRB exemption letter.

scenes.title: Anonymous, anonymized, coded, de-identified
scenes.altText: Identifiability ladder (ICH E15, as issued by FDA): identified (name or ID number on the sample) → coded (a code, with a key held by someone) → anonymized (coded first, then the link to identifiers deleted) → anonymous (never labeled with identifiers and no coding key ever made). HIPAA card (45 CFR 164.514): de-identified means 18 listed identifier types removed (safe harbor) or an expert determination of very small risk; a covered entity may keep a re-identification code. Exemption card: 46.104(d)(4) secondary-research exemptions include publicly available information, information recorded so identity cannot readily be ascertained with no contact and no re-identification, and certain HIPAA-regulated uses — so exempt does not always mean de-identified. Hook answers: (1) one case: usually not research, follow local policy and get publication consent; (2) a second case or series: ask the IRB under local policy before collecting more; (3) the five-year pull: follow the institution’s exemption process before data are pulled, rather than self-declaring.

cues.text: Now the data words. Anonymous data were never labeled with identifiers, and no key was ever made. Anonymized data were coded first, then the link was deleted. Coded data still have a key.
Under HIPAA, de-identified means removing eighteen listed identifier types, or an expert finding that the risk of identifying someone is very small. The entity may even keep a re-identification code.
Exempt is not the same as de-identified: the secondary-research exemption also covers public information and some HIPAA-regulated uses.

Back to the hook. One case: usually not research, but follow local policy and get consent to publish. The second case: ask the IRB first. The five-year pull: follow your institution’s exemption process before any data are pulled.

props.title: Hook answers
lines: 1 One case: local policy + consent to publish
2 Second case: ask the IRB first

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Federal rules say a second case makes it research” (✓ the number is not defined in the regulations; IRBs set it locally — ask before collecting more cases); “I can declare my own study exempt” (✓ the regulation does not name the decider; institutional policy does, and some require a formal IRB exemption letter); “Anonymous and de-identified mean the same” (✓ anonymous: never identified, no key; de-identified: identifiers removed later, and a code may still exist).

cues.text: Trap one: a federal rule says the second case makes it research. Not quite: the regulations set no number. Your IRB sets it, so ask before collecting more cases.
Trap two: I can declare my own study exempt. No: who decides is set by institutional policy, and some institutions require a formal IRB exemption letter.
Trap three: anonymous and de-identified are the same. No: anonymous data never had identifiers; de-identified data had them removed, and a code may still exist.

scenes.title: Snapshot, album, negatives
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “One case is a SNAPSHOT; a run of cases is an ALBUM you are curating — ask the IRB before you start collecting. Anonymous photos were taken with no names at all; de-identified photos had the names cut off, and someone may still hold the NEGATIVES (the code key).” Tokens: snapshot = one case · album = series · negatives = key. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: one case is a snapshot. A run of cases is an album you are curating, so ask the IRB before collecting. Anonymous photos never had names; de-identified photos had names cut off, and someone may still hold the negatives, the code key.

Where it breaks: the case count that makes an album is set locally; even a snapshot needs consent to publish; and HIPAA de-identification means removing eighteen identifier types or an expert finding, not just cutting off the name.

HIPAA: 18 identifier types, not just name

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “One case report: usually not research · more cases: local IRB threshold, ask before collecting”, “Exemption: institution decides · anonymous = never identified · de-identified = identifiers removed, code may remain”.

cues.text: A single case report is usually not research, but the case count that becomes research and who grants exemption are set by local policy, so ask the IRB before collecting data, and remember that anonymous data never had identifiers while de-identified data had them removed.

props.label: 1 case: usually not research · more: local IRB threshold, ask first

explanation.what: Plain language: writing up one interesting patient is usually seen as describing care, not doing research, but once you start gathering cases to find a pattern you may be doing research, and your institution decides where that line is and whether a study can skip full review. Data with no names are not all alike: some never had names, some had names removed, and some can still be traced back with a key. Scientific terms: Common Rule, research (systematic investigation, generalizable knowledge), human subject, identifiable private information, case report, case series, exempt research, secondary research, identified, single-coded, double-coded, anonymized, anonymous, HIPAA de-identification (safe harbor, expert determination), re-identification code.
explanation.why: The federal definition of research does not count cases, so institutions set their own thresholds and exemption procedures, and these differ from one institution to the next. Data labels matter because they decide whether results can be traced back to a person, which affects privacy risk, withdrawal and whether the activity involves human subjects at all.
explanation.measure: Research = systematic investigation designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge (46.102(l)). Human subject includes obtaining or analyzing identifiable private information (46.102(e)). Number of cases that makes research: not defined in the CFR; set locally. Federally supported covered research may not begin before IRB approval is certified (46.103(d)). Exempt categories: 46.104(d); (d)(4) includes public information, information recorded without readily ascertainable identity (no contact, no re-identification), and certain HIPAA-regulated uses. HIPAA de-identification: 18 identifier types removed or expert determination; re-identification code permitted (164.514(b)–(c)).
explanation.differs: Single descriptive case report (generally not research) vs case series or systematic chart review (can become research past a locally set threshold); exempt vs not human subjects research; anonymous (never identified, no key) vs anonymized (key deleted later) vs coded (key exists) vs HIPAA de-identified (identifiers removed; code may remain).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: decide whether a case report or series needs IRB involvement, pick who determines exemption, or define anonymous versus de-identified data.

mnemonic.text: One case is a SNAPSHOT; a run of cases is an ALBUM you are curating — ask the IRB before you start collecting. Anonymous photos were taken with no names at all; de-identified photos had the names cut off, and someone may still hold the NEGATIVES (the code key).
mnemonic.explanation: Snapshot vs album separates a case report from a case series; negatives stand for the code key that can still link de-identified data to a person.
mnemonic.limitation: The case count that makes an album is set locally; even a single case needs consent to publish; HIPAA de-identification requires removing 18 identifier types or an expert determination, not just the name; ICH “anonymized” means the key is deleted, unlike HIPAA de-identified data that may keep a code.

analogyLimitations: US federal rules only (Common Rule, HIPAA), paraphrased; read the current regulation and your institution’s policy.
takeaway: A single case report is usually not research, but the case count that becomes research and who grants exemption are set by local policy, so ask the IRB before collecting data, and remember that anonymous data never had identifiers while de-identified data had them removed.

questions.stem: A laboratory scientist wants to publish a report describing the clinical and laboratory features of one patient with a rare finding. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: It is generally not human subjects research, but local policy and the patient’s consent to publication still apply
options.rationale: Correct. A single descriptive case report generally does not meet the definition of human subjects research, yet institutional practice varies and many journals separately require the patient’s consent to publish.

options.text: It always requires full-board IRB review
options.rationale: Incorrect. A single descriptive case report is generally not treated as human subjects research, so mandatory full-board review does not follow.

options.text: No consent or privacy protection is needed because it is not research
options.rationale: Incorrect. Not being research does not remove the need for the patient’s consent to publish; many journals require consent documentation.

options.text: It becomes research because it will be published
options.rationale: Incorrect. Research is defined by systematic investigation designed for generalizable knowledge; the intent to publish does not make a project research.

questions.stem: Specimens were collected without any personal identifiers, and no coding key was ever created. Under ICH E15 terms, these specimens are:

options.rationale: Correct. Anonymous samples were never labeled with identifiers and no key was generated.
Incorrect. Anonymized samples were coded first and the link to identifiers was deleted later.
Incorrect. Single-coded samples can be traced back with a coding key.
Incorrect. Identified samples carry personal identifiers such as a name.

questions.stem: An investigator plans to review the records of 12 patients with a rare finding and believes the project is exempt. What is the best next step?

options.text: Submit it through the institution’s IRB process for a determination before pulling any data
options.rationale: Correct. The case-count threshold and who decides exemption are set by institutional policy, and some institutions require a formal IRB exemption letter, so asking first avoids starting a project that needs review.

options.text: Declare it exempt and start collecting data
options.rationale: Incorrect. Self-declaring risks starting a project that needs review; institutional policy sets who makes the call.

options.text: Collect the data now and contact the IRB before publishing
options.rationale: Incorrect. If the project is research needing review, checking only before publication is too late; federally supported covered research may not begin before IRB approval is certified.

options.text: Skip any review because the records already exist
options.rationale: Incorrect. Using identifiable private information from existing records can still be human subjects research.

claims.text: Common Rule definitions of research and human subject; federally supported covered research not begun before IRB approval is certified.
A single descriptive case report is generally not human subjects research; the case-count threshold is not in the CFR and is set locally by most IRBs; institutional practice varies.
Consent to publish personal details is a separate question from ethics review; many journals require consent documentation.

Exempt categories (46.104(d)(4)) include public, non-readily-identifiable and certain HIPAA-regulated data; 46.104 does not name the decider; institutional policy governs and some institutions require formal IRB exemption letters.
Identified, coded, anonymized, anonymous (ICH E15); HIPAA de-identification by safe harbor (18 identifier types) or expert determination, with a permitted re-identification code.
Reviewer’s rules stated as universal: “a second case = research” and “the IRB, never the investigator, decides exemption”; trial phases, Moore v. UCLA, kickbacks, research billing.
claims.note: Not taught as federal rules; the lesson teaches them as local-policy matters. Other items not taught in this lesson.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer states that a second case makes a report a systematic investigation requiring IRB review. The US regulations do not define a case count; most IRBs set a local threshold and practice varies (Bass 2020; Valešić 2025). The lesson teaches the threshold as local policy.

The reviewer describes exempt studies as using deidentified, already-collected data. 45 CFR 46.104(d)(4) also exempts secondary research on publicly available identifiable information and certain HIPAA-regulated uses of identifiable health information; data that are not identifiable may fall outside the human-subject definition altogether.

The reviewer’s anonymous vs deidentified distinction matches the ICH E15 anonymous vs anonymized categories, but HIPAA de-identified data may still carry a re-identification code held by the covered entity, and de-identification requires removing 18 identifier types or an expert determination.
The lesson describes US federal rules (Common Rule, HIPAA). Philippine research-ethics and data-privacy requirements are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.
